sections.html:
Zanesville is the Muskingum County seat, roughly 52 miles east of Columbus, at the junction of two rivers. The population is 25,138. Renters outnumber owners here: owner occupancy is 43.8%, the median home value is $123,700, and median gross rent is $821.

With fewer than half of homes lived in by their owners, tenants are part of many sales. If your house has a tenant, tell buyers whether the lease runs past closing and who holds the deposit. Interstate 70 and U.S. 40 both run through town, which keeps commuters and travelers in the local buyer pool.

The city's Building and Code Enforcement office, at 401 Market Street, Room 227, enforces the International Property Maintenance Code, the city's codified ordinances and the zoning code. It can start legal proceedings against violators. The doors are open weekdays from 7:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. Reach them at 740-617-4890.

The same office issues and inspects the permits a buyer's inspector will ask about:

  • Residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, which do not include plumbing.
  • Residential and commercial sidewalk, curb and curb cut permits.
  • Demolition permits.
  • Permits to move a house or an accessory structure wider than 14 feet or larger than 450 square feet.
  • Certificates of occupancy.

The office keeps lists of condemned properties and posts a 2026 annual vacant property form. If your house sits empty, ask whether the form applies to you before you list. For zoning questions, call Planning and Zoning at 740-617-4909. If your address is just outside the city line, South Zanesville has its own permit department at 740-454-0492.

sections.h2: Values, appeals and homestead in Muskingum County
sections.html:
For valuation and exemption questions, the Muskingum County Auditor is at the courthouse, 401 Main Street, (740) 455-7109, open weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The January 2026 tax bills reflect values set in January 2025. An addition, a demolition or newly passed levies can change a bill.

Appealing your value

Values are adjusted by the Board of Revision, which has three members: the auditor, the treasurer and the president of the commissioners, or people they designate. It cannot change how many tax dollars the county collects. Your complaint is a formal legal filing handed to the auditor between January 1 and March 31. Plan on one complaint every three years, and note that pulling one back still uses up your turn. What to expect:

  • You carry the burden of proof. The board can raise your value, cut it or leave it unchanged.
  • The hearing notice arrives by certified mail at least ten days ahead.
  • After a filing, an appraiser from the auditor may visit and propose a settlement figure. Accepting it in writing cancels the hearing.
  • A corporation should have an attorney file for it.

Homestead exemption

The Homestead Exemption is for seniors, disabled owners and surviving spouses. For tax year 2025 it takes $29,000 off taxable market value, with an income limit of $41,000 that is adjusted each year for inflation. The filing deadline is December 31. A disabled-veteran owner gets a larger reduction, equal to the tax on up to $58,000 of market value. If you receive the exemption, ask the auditor how a sale affects it on your parcel.

sections.h2: What a Zanesville seller must disclose
sections.html:
Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, anyone selling a one to four unit home completes a state disclosure form. Answer honestly and deliver it quickly. Errors about things you did not actually know of do not create liability for you. If the buyer gets the form late, though, they may cancel within three business days.

Gather permit numbers and any notices from the code office before showings, so the buyer sees them alongside the form. Open permits, a condemned notice or an unfiled vacant property form are the sort of loose ends that slow a closing.

sections.h2: Before you list: a short checklist
sections.html:
Make a handful of calls before the sign goes up. The city code office can tell you which permits a deck, addition, furnace or electrical panel needed, and whether an empty house must file the vacant form. The county auditor can explain your value, your homestead status and whether the January bills picked up a recent change.

Next, pull together the paperwork a buyer will want: the deed, any lease and deposit records if a tenant lives there, receipts for major repairs, and the permit numbers noted above. Fill out the state disclosure form early and slowly, since rushed answers are where honest mistakes creep in. If the house is vacant, walk through it for anything the code office could cite, such as overgrown yards, broken steps or boarded openings, and fix what you can before photos are taken.

Planning an appeal? The window shuts on March 31. If a sale could close before then, ask the auditor what happens to a pending complaint once the parcel changes owners.

sections.h2: When a cash offer makes sense
sections.html:
Consider a cash offer for a rental with tenant trouble, an inherited house or a place whose repairs would worry a lender's appraiser. It can also end the monthly cost of a vacant house that keeps drawing taxes and utility bills. With cash there is usually no lender appraisal to pass and fewer repair demands after inspection.

The usual steps are simple. First you describe the house. Then a buyer makes an offer, often after a walk-through, and you choose the closing day. A title company prepares the paperwork and records the deed. Tenants, unpaid code citations and an incomplete permit history do not disappear in a cash sale, so settle what you can with the city first and be upfront about the rest.

If your house has open code issues, ask each buyer how they would treat them and get the answer in writing before you pick a closing date. Many buyers will take a property as it stands, but read what the contract says about repairs, access and the deposit.

Get at least two written offers, line up the closing costs and dates side by side, and request the settlement statement from the title company a day or two ahead of signing.

faqs.q: Who do I call about zoning in Zanesville?
faqs.a: Zoning questions go to the city's Planning and Zoning office, 740-617-4909. South Zanesville and several townships have separate contacts, since zoning follows the address.

faqs.q: How often can I appeal my Muskingum County property value?
faqs.a: About once every three years. The filing window is January 1 to March 31, and a complaint you withdraw still counts as your turn.

faqs.q: Can the Board of Revision raise my value?
faqs.a: Yes, it can go up. Since you must prove your case, bring a recent comparable sale, an appraisal or repair estimates.

faqs.q: Does a vacant house need to be registered?
faqs.a: The city posts an annual vacant property form for 2026. Call 740-617-4890 to learn whether your address must file before a sale.

faqs.q: What permits might a buyer ask me about?
faqs.a: A buyer's inspector may ask about residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, demolition permits and certificates of occupancy. All are issued by the city's Building and Code Enforcement office, so bring permit numbers for any addition or major system replacement.
